Priyanshu, here's the constraint engineering breakdown using your actual prompt as the case study.

---

## Part 1: Your Missing Constraints — Before & After

### Missing Constraint #1: No Scope Lock

**What you wrote:**
> "You have to create whole new, better skills by understanding the intent of these skills by reading them."

**The problem:** "Better" has no definition. Better how? Shorter? More accurate? Faster to trigger? The agent picks its own definition of "better" and optimizes for something you might not care about.

**How to constrain it:**
> "Read prompt-forge/SKILL.md. Create a new skill file called prompt-forge-v2/SKILL.md. The new skill must: (1) be under 200 lines, (2) keep the CREATE and ENHANCE modes, (3) add a new GAP ANALYSIS output mode. Do not modify the original file. Do not touch anti-sycophancy or deep-researcher in this task."

**The rule:** Every task needs a **boundary box** — what files to touch, what NOT to touch, and a measurable definition of the output.

---

### Missing Constraint #2: No Stop Condition

**What you wrote:**
> "find a sweet spot for this so that any work I am doing gets the best possible response a model can give"

**The problem:** "Best possible response" has no ceiling. The agent will keep researching, rewriting, expanding, second-guessing. There is no signal that says "you're done now."

**How to constrain it:**
> "Optimize the anti-sycophancy skill for these 3 specific use cases: (1) YouTube script review, (2) web research synthesis, (3) business proposal drafting. For each use case, write one example showing how the skill changes the agent's behavior. Stop after the 3 examples."

**The rule:** Always define **what "done" looks like**. Either a deliverable count ("3 examples"), a size limit ("under 150 lines"), or a completion signal ("stop after generating the SKILL.md file").

---

### Missing Constraint #3: No Priority Ordering

**What you wrote:**
> "So, not just for anti-sycophancy, you can just audit all that first and find out which things should not
<truncated 4597 bytes>
ons about instructions:** "If I have given you some wrong prompts, tell me"

The agent has to parse all of this, figure out which parts are actionable tasks vs. context vs. philosophy vs. questions — and it gets confused. It tries to address ALL of them.

**What works instead:** Separate your meta-thoughts from your task. Put behavioral instructions in your skills/rules (which you already did with anti-sycophancy). Put task instructions in the prompt. Don't mix them.

---

### Mistake #3: Asking the Agent to Replace Its Own Tools

> "you can make better than this deep research slash skills that you are using right now"

You asked the agent to use `/deep-research` AND simultaneously build a replacement for `/deep-research`. That's like asking a carpenter to build a house while also redesigning the hammer mid-swing. The agent can't use a tool and critique it at the same time in the same session — it creates a logical conflict where the agent doesn't know whether to trust its own research pipeline or question it.

**What works instead:** Use the tool in one session, evaluate the output yourself, then in a **separate session** say:
> "Here's the output from deep-researcher. Here's what was wrong with it: [specific problems]. Fix these specific issues in a new version of the skill."

Your evaluation of the output is the input for the improvement. Don't ask the tool to evaluate itself.

---

## Quick Reference Card

Next time, before you hit Enter, run this checklist:

```
□ Is this ONE task or multiple? → Split if multiple
□ Did I define "done"?          → Add stop condition
□ Did I specify output shape?   → Table / list / file / N bullet points
□ Did I set a size limit?       → Lines / words / sources
□ Did I sequence the steps?     → "First X, then Y, wait between"
□ Did I remove flattery?        → Replace with role assignment
□ Did I separate meta from task? → Behavioral stuff goes in skills, not prompts
```

That's it. These 7 checks would have prevented the session blowup entirely.
